Page 276

In another narration from him, it is the name of each of seven mountains encircling the seven earths, one behind another, just as the seven earths are one earth behind another. That is, it is a generic noun whose instances are confined to seven. Was it not enough for them that it is written in the form of the disjointed letters like: Alif Lam Mim, Ta Sin Mim, Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad? And if the imagined mountain were intended, it would have been written qaf as three letters, just as the names of things are written, such as 'ayn (the eye, the organ) and ghayn (the verbal noun of "ghana 'alayhi"). It is not correct to indicate these names by the letters of spelling, as is not hidden.

The pronoun in "they wonder" refers to an unmentioned antecedent, whose referent is known from the context, namely the opening of the surah with the letter of spelling, by which the purpose was to make them unable to produce the like of the Qur'an, because their inability to produce its like, while it is composed of the letters of their own language, indicates to them that it is not the speech of a human, but is speech originated by God's power and conveyed by God to His messenger ﷺ through the angel. The challengers to miraculousness are well known, and the Muslims know them, and they too know that they are the ones meant by the challenge of miraculousness. Moreover, what will explain the pronoun will come in His words: "the disbelievers said."

The pronoun in "from themselves" refers to the same antecedent as the pronoun in "they wonder." The meaning is that he is of their kind, that is, of the children of Adam.

"That a warner has come to them" is in the genitive governed by the omitted (min) with (an), that is, they wondered at the coming of a warner from among them, or they wondered at the claim that a warner has come to them from among themselves.

It was what deceived them, so they deemed it impossible that God would send to them anyone of their own kind. For this reason, the Messenger ﷺ was first described with the attribute "warner" before being described as being from among them, to show that what he warned them of was the original motive for their denial of him, and that his being from among them only strengthened their far-fetched view and wonder.

Then this leads to refuting their argument and establishing resurrection, which is the aim of His words: ﴿We know what the earth diminishes of them﴾ [Qaf: 4] up to His words "thus is the coming forth."

Within these two verses are many features of eloquence: among them the concise omission; among them what the reversal conveys of concern for the matter of resurrection; among them the striking concision resulting from the expression "warner"; among them the insertion of describing him as from among them, because this has a role in their wonder; among them the use of the noun in place of the pronoun contrary to what the apparent context requires; and among them the summary followed by detail in His words: "This is a strange thing. When we have died..." and so on.

He expressed them by the explicit noun in "the disbelievers said" rather than "they said," to brand them, for this statement is among the effects of disbelief, and so that it would serve as an explanation of the two earlier pronouns.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 50, verse 4:

﴿We have indeed known what the earth diminishes of them, and with Us is a Book preserved.﴾

This is a rebuttal of their saying, "That is a far-off return" (Q. 50:3). Their denial of the resurrection arises from several doubts. Among them: the scattering of the parts of bodies across the expanses of the earth and the directions of the winds leaves no hope that they can be gathered, since no one encompasses them; and even if their locations were known, gathering them would be impossible; and even if they were gathered, how could they return to the forms in which they were once constituted; and even if they returned, how could they return into them. So, in dispelling their doubts, He confined Himself to uprooting their source, which is the lack of knowledge of the locations of those parts and their particles.

The sentence is separated without a conjunction because it is the beginning of a speech that answers their speech, and this is the most fitting for the arrangement of the discourse.

It has also been said that it is the answer to the oath, as you have learned just now. In either case, it is a rebuttal of their saying: ﴿That is a far-off return﴾ [Q. 50:3].

The meaning is: the gathering of the parts of bodies is possible and is not hidden from the knowledge of God. Since He is knowing of those parts, as the generality of divine knowledge requires, and since He has willed to revive their owners, as He has informed, the gathering of them and their composition into bodies like the bodies of their owners at the time they departed from life is not difficult for His power. So His saying ﴿We have indeed known what the earth diminishes of them﴾ is an indication of the proof of possibility, because it reverts to the generality of knowledge, as we have said.

Thus the foundation of the structure of the rebuttal is the generality of God's knowledge, the Exalted, because it encompasses the nullification of the possibilities that arise from their doubt. For if He had said, "We are capable of returning what the earth diminishes of them," there would have occurred to the whisperings of their souls the doubt that God, even if we grant that He is capable, does not know the parts of bodies once they are scattered, until His power is brought to bear on gathering them. So building upon the generality of knowledge was more decisive against their possibilities.

Know that this statement is an explanation of possibility, in consideration of what their speech contained of impossibility, because the establishment of possibility uproots the belief in impossibility from their souls, and it is sufficient to nullify their denial and to invite them to consider the call. Then the consideration of the manner of the restoration remains, which is a matter we have not been charged to investigate. The leading scholars of the Ahl al-Sunnah have differed concerning it. The majority of the Ahl al-Sunnah and the Mu'tazilah said: bodies are restored after their non-existence. The meaning of their restoration is the restoration of their likenesses, by God creating bodies like the first, into which are deposited the spirits that were in the world, inhering in the bodies that are now non-existent. Thus that body becomes the body of the owner of the spirit in the world, and by this it is right to say: this is so-and-so whom we knew in the world, since the human being was a human by reason and speech, and these are the manifestation of the spirit. As for the body, it changes through many changes, beginning from the time it was an embryo, then from the time of childhood, and then the stages after that, so its renewed parts replace its departed parts. The proof of this is explained in the science of natural philosophy. Yet that change does not prevent regarding the essence as one essence, because the identity of the essence is achieved from the specific reality and the observed individuating features, which are renewed without the awareness of the one who observes them.

Therefore, the reality of the person is the spirit, and it is that which is clothed at the resurrection in the body of its owner in the world. For the people who die shortly before the Hour, whose bodies do not decay in such a short time, their spirits return to their remaining bodies without renewed creation of them. Accordingly, naming this bringing-into-being a ma'ad (return), or raj' (return), or ba'th (resurrection) is only a naming with regard to the state of the spirits. And by this same consideration their tongues, hands and feet testify against the unbelievers regarding what they used to do, because the true witness is that by which the works are perceived, namely the spirit spread through the limbs.

Most of the evidences of the Book clearly support this opinion, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿As We originated the first creation, We shall repeat it﴾ [Q. 21:104], and in its meaning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Every time their skins are roasted through, We will replace them with other skins, that they may taste the punishment﴾ [Q. 4:56].

A deviant view said: bodies are restored by gathering the scattered parts, which God, who knows them, gathers and assembles as they were on the day of death. This is far-fetched, because when the parts of the human body are scattered, they enter into parts of other bodies of various existents, among them the bodies of other people.

It is reported in the traditions: "Every son of Adam decays except the coccyx, from which he was created and from which he will be assembled," narrated by Muslim. On this basis, the relation of the restored bodies is like the relation of the palm tree to the date-stone. This is an intermediate position between the view that restoration is from non-existence and the view that it is from dispersion.

No intelligent person holds that what is non-existent is restored in its very self; what is meant is what we have mentioned, and anything else is careless expression.

Al-Jalal al-Dawani, in his commentary on the 'Adudiyyah creed, mentions that Ubayy ibn Khalaf, when he heard what the Qur'an says about resurrection, came to the Prophet (ﷺ) holding a bone that had decayed, crumbled it in his hand and said: "O Muhammad, do you think God will revive me after I become like this bone?" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Yes, and He will resurrect you and cause you to enter the Fire." And concerning him was revealed His saying: ﴿And he struck for Us a parable and forgot his own creation. He said: Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?﴾ [Q. 36:78].

The phrase "what the earth diminishes" was used instead of expressing it as annihilation, because bodies have degrees of dissolution that fall under the reality of diminution. Some parts of the body may perish while others remain, and perishing may come upon all its parts. Moreover, if it is sound that the coccyx does not perish, then the perishing of bodies is a diminution, not an annihilation.

Coupled to His saying ﴿We have indeed known what the earth diminishes of them﴾ is His saying: "and with Us is a Book preserved," as a coordination of the more general over the more specific, and it has the sense of an appendix (tadhyil) to the clause ﴿We have indeed known what the earth diminishes of them﴾, meaning: with Us is knowledge of everything, firmly established. The indefiniteness of "Book" is for magnification, and it is the magnification of generality, meaning: with Us is the book of everything.

"Hafiz" is an intensive form (fa'il), which may be in the sense of the active participle, meaning: preserving what has been appointed for its enumeration of the names of the essences and their destinies, and the determination of all spirits for their essences in which they were deposited, such that not one of them escapes the angels appointed for resurrection, the restoration of bodies and the infusing of spirits into them.

And it may be in the sense of the passive participle, meaning: what is in it is protected from what commonly befalls familiar books of erasure, alteration, addition, striking out, and the like.

"Kitab" means the written thing, and it is applied to the totality of pages.

Then it is permissible that "Kitab" be taken literally, in that God made books and deposited them with angels who record in them people at their deaths, the places of their bodies, the abodes of their spirits, and the attribution of each spirit to its specific body in which it dwelt during the life of this world, truly, with many books, each person having his own book. This would be like the records of deeds concerning which His saying, Exalted is He, came: ﴿When the two receivers receive, seated on the right and on the left﴾ [Q. 50:17], ﴿He utters no word except that with him is a watchful observer ready﴾ [Q. 50:18], and His saying: ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a book which he will find laid open﴾ [Q. 17:13], ﴿Read your book; sufficient is yourself against you this day as an accountant﴾ [Q. 17:14].

It is also permissible that the whole of His saying "and with Us is a Book" be a figure (tamthil) for God's knowledge, the Exalted, by way of the state of the knowledge of one who has with him a preserved book by which he knows all the deeds of people.

The "withness" in His saying "and with Us is a Book" is a metaphor for enclosing and preservation, lest anything reach it that would alter what is in it or anyone who would nullify what it has been appointed for.

﴿Nay, but they have denied the truth when it came to them, so they are in a confused state (amr marij).﴾

This is a second digression (idrab) that follows the digression in His saying: ﴿Nay, but they wonder that a warner has come to them from among themselves﴾ [Qaf: 2], following the method of repeating a sentence in a context of censure and refutation. Alternatively, it is a substitute (badal) for the sentence ﴿Nay, but they wonder that a warner has come to them﴾ [Qaf: 2], because that wonder includes denial. Both considerations require that this sentence be separated without a conjunction (ʿatf).

The purpose of this sentence is that they committed something more heinous than their denial of resurrection, and that is their denial of the truth.

The intended meaning of "the truth" (al-haqq) here is the Qur'an, because when the verb "to deny" (takdhib) is followed by the preposition bi-, it takes as its object the report (khabar), and when it is followed directly by its object, it is the denial of the one who reports.

(Lamma) is a particle of timing, indicating that the occurrence of its response is linked to the time of the occurrence of its condition. It therefore signifies that the response occurs immediately upon the occurrence of the condition, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when it lit up around him, Allah took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17], and His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89]. Both have passed in Surat al-Baqarah. The meaning of "came to them" (jaa'hum) is that it reached them and they were informed of it.

The meaning is that they hastened to deny without reflection or consideration of what it contained of the truth. Rather, they denied it from the very first moment, and so they denied the Oneness of Allah, which is the first truth the Qur'an brought. For this reason it is followed by His saying: ﴿Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We built it﴾ [Qaf: 6], up to His saying: ﴿And We revived by it a dead land﴾ [Qaf: 11].

Thus, denial of what the Qur'an brought encompasses denial of resurrection and other things.

Following on from the report to which the digression shifted, the description of their state, arising from their hastening to deny before reflection, is given as "a confused state" (amr marij), which surrounded them, and they were tossed about in it, as the particle of location indicates.

"Amr" (amr) is an indefinite noun like "shay'" (thing). Since it occurs here after the particle fi (in), which is used in a figurative sense of location, it is determined that the intended meaning of "amr" is the condition in which they are involved, as an enclosed thing is involved in what encloses it. The use of fi is therefore a subordinate (tabiyya) metaphor.

Page 285

"Marij" means agitated and confused, that is, there is no settledness within themselves in this denial. Their states were all agitated in it, from their statements describing the Qur'an: they rushed to deny it of truthfulness without clarifying which kind of false speech to attach to it. So they said: "Clear magic" (sihr mubin), and they said: "Myths of the ancients" (asatir al-awwalin), and they said: "The word of a poet," and they said: "The word of a soothsayer," and they said: it is the raving of a madman. This is also seen in their conduct in the ways of opposing the call of the Prophet ﷺ, and in what they would say about him when delegations from the Arab tribes came asking them. It also appears in their confusion regarding the inimitability of the Qur'an and the proof of other miracles, and in the arguments with which he refuted them, establishing the rejection of associating partners and affirming the Oneness of Allah. This is a reproach to them, that their minds were disordered, so they did not perfect their denial, nor did they settle on a description of the speech which they denied.

**[Page 286]**

This is a consequence (*tafri'*) of His saying: ﴿Nay, they marvel that a warner has come to them﴾ [Qaf: 2], up to His saying: "confused" [Qaf: 5], because the most important element of their denial was that they denied the Resurrection. The creation of the heavens, the stars and the earth shows that the return of the human being after non-existence is within the realm of possibility, since those worlds were brought into existence out of non-existence. Even more clearly indicating this is His saying in Surah Ya Sin: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ [Ya Sin: 81].

The interrogative (*istifham*) may be a rhetorical question of denial (*inkari*). The seeing (*nazar*) is reflective contemplation, as in His saying: ﴿Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [Yunus: 101].

The locus of the denial is the state indicated by "how We built it," meaning: Have they not reflected upon the signs of creation? So the verse has the same sense as: ﴿Have they not reflected within themselves? God did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾ [Rum: 8].

It is also possible that the interrogative is an affirmative question (*taqriri*), and that the seeing is direct observation. The locus of the affirmation is then the verb "they look," or "how" may be intended to refer to the observed state.

This is a Qur'anic method, which we have mentioned more than once: affirmation by means of a negation, where what is intended is the affirmation of the thing. We have explained that its purpose is to leave room for the one being addressed (*al-muqarrar*) if he wishes to deny what is affirmed to him, out of the confidence of the one who affirms (*al-muqarrir*, with a kasra on the ra') that the one affirmed (*al-muqarrar*, with a fatha on the ra') will not dare to reject what has been affirmed to him, because of its obviousness. This was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿Do they not see that it does not speak to them?﴾ [Al-A'raf: 148], and at His saying: "Am I not your Lord?" both in Surah al-A'raf.

This interpretation is stronger in rebuking them, because it implies that the indication of the mentioned creatures toward the possibility of resurrection is sufficient by mere sight with the eye.

"Above them" (*fawqahum*) is a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of "the heaven." Restricting it by this circumstance is a reproach against them for neglecting reflection while having the ability to do it, since the heaven is near, above them, and looking at it requires only raising their heads.

"How" (*kayfa*) is an invariable, indeclinable noun (*ism jamid mabni*) whose meaning is "state" (*halah*). It occurs most often in speech to ask about a state. It then functions as a predicate before what cannot be dispensed with, as in "How are you?" and as a circumstantial accusative before what can be dispensed with, as in "How did he come?" It also functions as an absolute object, as in "How did your Lord act?" and as a direct object, as in His saying: ﴿Look how We have favored some of them over others﴾ [Al-Isra': 21]. Here it is a substitute (*badal*) for "above them," and so it is a circumstantial qualifier in meaning. The sense is: Have they not looked at the heaven above them in the form in which We built it? The clause "We built it" then explains "how."

The term "building" (*bina'*) is applied to the creation of the heavenly bodies by the common feature of elevation.

By "the heaven" (*al-sama'*) is meant here what the eye sees of the sphere of air that appears like a dome and is called the atmosphere (*al-jaww*).

Adornment (*tazyin*) is making a thing an adornment, that is, beautifying it, meaning making its appearance pleasing to the beholder by what appears in it of the sun by day and the moon and stars by night.

He limited the sign to the adornment of the heaven, without detailing the signs in the stars with which it is adorned, because the adornment is perceived by all who see it, and in order to combine argument with the favor of enabling people to behold pleasing sights, as He said: ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home and when you drive them out to pasture﴾ [Al-Nahl: 6], concerning the creation of livestock in Surah al-Nahl.

Then people differ in perceiving what is in the creation of the stars, the sun, the moon and their order of signs, according to the degree to which their knowledge and intellects differ.

The verse is suitable for conveying meaning to all classes of people.

The clause ﴿and there are no fissures in it﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with the two clauses ﴿how We built it and adorned it﴾, so it is a third circumstantial qualifier in meaning.

"Fissures" (*furuj*) is the plural of *farj*, which means a break or rift. That is, they see it as a sphere whose parts are connected, with no disparity among its parts that would appear as a rift, nor any separation that would split part of it from another so as to form a break in its dome.

This is among the wonders of craftsmanship: a massive body, like the body of the atmospheric air sphere, is made as if cast in a mold.

This is observed by all classes of people, despite the differences in their perceptions, and then they differ in perceiving the wonders of this craftsmanship in the harmonious unity of the sphere of air surrounding the earth.

Had there been in the surface of what is called the heaven any inconsistency among its parts, fissures, depressions and elevations would have appeared in it. A parallel to this verse is His saying in Surah al-Mulk: ﴿He who created seven heavens in layers﴾ [Al-Mulk: 3], up to His saying: ﴿Do you see any flaw?﴾ [Al-Mulk: 3].

[p. 288]

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause "Have they not looked?" as a statement coordinated with an interrogative of denial (istifham inkari), which carries the sense of an assertion. The implied sense is: "And We spread out the earth."

Since the conditions of the earth are before people's eyes and are nearer to them than the conditions of the heavens, because they appear to the sight without effort, the verse does not use an interrogative of denial to draw their attention to its signs. This treats them as one who has already considered the conditions of the earth, so they have no need to be reminded of them again.

"Al-ʾArḍa" (the earth) is in the accusative, governed by "madadnāhā" (We spread it), in the construction called ishtighal (the verb is elided and its pronoun object is attached to the verb).

Al-madd (spreading) is extending, that is, We spread out the earth, so it is not a collection of protrusions, for if it were so, walking on it would be exhausting.

What is meant is the spreading of the surface of the earth, not a description of the earth's size, because that is not perceived by observation, and the addressees did not look at it with careful reflection so that they could be given a proof based on something they do not know. It is therefore not relevant in the context of proof of the power to create great things, nor in the context of the favour contained in that sign. Thus this verse has no connection with the question of the earth's sphericity.

Al-ibqāʾ (here: "wa-alqaynā," and We cast) is a figurative expression (tamthīl) for the formation of protruding bodies on the earth, spaced apart from one another, because the literal sense of al-ilqāʾ is throwing something from the hand onto the ground. This is an argument from the creation of mountains, as in His saying: ﴿And at the mountains, how they are set up?﴾ (88:19). "Fīhā" is a stable adverbial phrase (ẓarf mustaqarr) serving as a description of "rawāsī" (firm mountains). It has been placed before the word it describes, so it became a circumstantial (ḥāl). It may also be a free adverbial phrase (ẓarf laghw) connected to "alqaynā."

Rawāsī is the plural of rāsin, in an irregular pattern, like fawāris and ʿawādhil.

Al-rusūw is steadiness and stability.

The benefit of this description is to draw further attention to the wondrous creation of God, in that He made the mountains integrated with the earth and not placed upon it in the manner that a tent is pitched, for if they were like that, they would shake, collapse, and destroy what surrounds them.

He said in Surat al-Anbiyāʾ: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains lest it sway with you﴾ (16:15), meaning: He repelled the earth from swaying, that is, the mountains prevent it from swaying with you, meaning they are attached to you in its swaying. There is another interpretation, which was discussed in Surat al-Anbiyāʾ.

Al-zawj (pair, kind) is a type of animal, fruit or plant. It was already mentioned in His saying: ﴿So We brought forth with it pairs of various plants﴾ (20:53) in Surat Ṭāhā.

[p. 289]

The meaning: "And We made to grow in the earth kinds and types of plants."

His saying "min kulli zawjin" (of every kind) shows that the particle "min" in it is redundant, for emphasis. The redundancy of "min" in non-negated statements is rare, meaning that it is less frequent than its redundancy in negated statements. However, its redundancy in affirmative statements occurs in eloquent speech. The grammarians of Kufa, al-Akhfash, Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī and Ibn Jinnī permitted analogy upon it. From it is His saying: ﴿And He sends down from the sky mountains of hail in which is hail﴾ (24:43). The meaning is: He sends down from the sky mountains containing hail.

This has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathes﴾ (6:99) in Surat al-Anʿām.

Therefore the purpose of the emphasis by the particle "min" is to place them in the position of one who denies that God caused to grow on the earth every kind of thing, when they claimed the impossibility of bringing people out of the earth. For this reason emphasis was used in this verse, because the discourse in it concerns the polytheists, and emphasis was not used in the verse of Surat Ṭāhā.

The "min" here is not partitive (lil-tabʿīḍ), because that is not the intended meaning.

The word "kull" (every) is used to mean abundance, as already discussed in His saying: ﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾ (6:25) in Surat al-Anʿām, and His saying in it: ﴿And if they offer every ransom, it will not be accepted from them﴾ (6:70). This is like His saying: ﴿So We brought forth with it pairs of various plants﴾ (20:53) in Surat Ṭāhā.

The benefit of abundance here is to rebuke them for their scant reflection, since they were blind to many clear signs before them.

Al-bahīj may be an adjective of the form faʿīl (a stable attribute), from "bahuja" with the vowel u on the ha, meaning it became pleasing in the eyes of onlookers. Thus al-bahīj means in the sense of the active participle, as indicated by His saying: ﴿So We caused to grow with it gardens of delight﴾ (27:60).

It may also be faʿīl in the sense of passive participle (maf'ūl), meaning "mubhaj bihi" (one by which joy is caused), with an elision and transfer (of the preposition), meaning that the onlooker is delighted by it. It is said: "bahajahu," from the pattern of "manaʿa," when it gladdened him. From this comes al-ibtihāj, which is gladness.

The mention of this description serves to strengthen the argument for the precision of God's craftsmanship, and to include the favour upon them through it, so that they would give thanks for the blessing and not reject it by worshipping other than Him, as in His saying: ﴿And the livestock, He created them for you; in them is warmth and benefits, and from them you eat﴾ (16:5). ﴿And for you in them is beauty when you bring them home in the evening and when you send them out to pasture﴾ (16:6).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 50, verse 8:

﴿As an insight and a reminder for every servant who turns back (to Allah) in repentance.﴾

It is an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi, the object of purpose or "object of cause") for the preceding verbs in His saying: "We built it and adorned it," and His saying "We spread it out," and ﴿We placed firm mountains upon it and caused to grow therein﴾ [Qaf: 7], etc., on the basis that it is a cause for them, in a manner of the method of tanazu' (the grammatical dispute over a shared element between verbs). That is, so that what was mentioned of the verbs and their objects would be an insight and a reminder, meaning: We made it for the purpose that We would give insight by it and remind every servant who turns back.

He omitted the complement of "insight and reminder" so that it would encompass everything that may be contemplated concerning the signs of the creation of the earth and what is upon it. The most important of that for them is Tawhid (the oneness of God) and resurrection, as the context indicates explicitly and allusively.

It is necessary in the weak (defective) root, as in: zakka tazkiyatan and ghattaahu taghtiyatan.

Al-dhikra (reminder) is a verbal noun of dhakara, when one causes someone to remember what he has forgotten. It is used here for the soul's reviewing what it had known and then became heedless of.

"'Abd" (servant) here means the servant of Allah, i.e., a created being, and it is applied only to human beings. Its plural is 'ibad, not 'abid.

Al-munib (the one who turns back) is the one who returns; the intended meaning here is the one who returns to the truth through obedience to Allah. When he deviates, or some preoccupation occupies him, he hastens to return to the state of uprightness and compliance he was in, so the state of obedience never leaves him, and if it leaves him for a little while, he returns to it and turns back in repentance.

The application of al-munib to the penitent and of inabah (turning back) to tawbah (repentance) are among the branches of this meaning, and it was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿And he fell down bowing and turned back﴾ [Sad: 24] in Surah Sad.

The servant who turns back is singled out for the insight and reminder, although these conditions of the earth provide insight and reminder to everyone, because the servant who turns back is the one who benefits from this, so he is, as it were, the intended one in the wisdom of those acts. This is an honouring of the believers and an allusion to the neglect of the disbelievers in contemplating and remembering. The word "kull" (every) is taken in its literal meaning of encompassing and inclusiveness. The meaning is: those acts were intended to provide insight and reminder to all the servants who follow the truth, since they do not lack insight and reminder through those acts, though they differ in that degree.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 50, verse 9–10:

﴿And We send down from the sky blessed water, and We produce thereby gardens and the grain of harvest.﴾ ﴿And tall palm trees with ranged spathes.﴾

After the contemplation, the reminder, and the enlightenment regarding the making of the heavens, the making of the earth, and what is in them since their origination, the speech moved to the reminder of the bringing into existence of effects from the effects of those created things, which are renewed over the passage of time: living, then dying, then living again, continually. Al-mubarak (the blessed) is the passive participle of one in whom blessing (baraka) has been placed, meaning that abundant good has been placed in it.

صفحة ٢٩٢
The verbs of this root are highly varied in usage and diverse in their construction. Baraka is beneficial good by which there results the growth of grains, grapes and palm trees. If the creation of the heavens and what is in them, the spreading of the earth, and the placing of mountains in it are signs of the great power of the Lord because the modes of their formation are hidden, then the manifestation of the modes of formation in the sending down of water and the occurrence of growth and fruiting is a proof of the great knowledge of God, exalted is He.

**Ka-dhalika al-khuruj** (Thus is the coming forth) — after the evidences have appeared through God's craftsmanship, proving the possibility of resurrection, because the creation of those creatures from nothing shows that the renewal of some weak existing things is more possible and easier. He used what conveys bringing the resurrection near, with his statement "ka-dhalika al-khuruj."

This sentence is a conclusion (fadhlakah) of the argument for the possibility of resurrection, which the preceding sentences contained. Therefore this sentence is separated, so it is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) or a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) at the end of the speech according to the opinion of those who permit it, and this is the more correct view.

The demonstrative "dhalika" refers to what was mentioned just before, the giving of life to the land after its death: as We gave life to the land after its death, so We will bring people to life after their death and decay. Along with conveying the magnification of the status of what is pointed to, that is, the like of the great resurrection is the great origination.

The definiteness of "al-khuruj" is for a known reference, namely the coming forth of people from the earth, as He, may He be exalted, said

**﴿Yawma yakhrujuna mina al-ajdathi sira'an﴾** [al-Ma'arij: 43]. So "al-khuruj" became like a proper name by dominance for the resurrection, and His statement will come: **﴿Dhalika yawmu al-khuruji﴾** [Qaf: 42].

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the subject is for the sake of emphasizing the predicate, because in the predicate there is removal of impossibility and manifestation of nearness, and in it is a stimulus for the listener to receive the predicated element.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 50, verses 12–14:

﴿Before them the people of Noah denied, and the companions of the Rass, and Thamud,﴾ ﴿and 'Ad, and Pharaoh, and the brothers of Lot,﴾ ﴿and the companions of the Thicket, and the people of Tubba'. Each one denied the messengers, so My warning came true.﴾

This is a fresh, independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) arising from His saying: "Nay, they denied the truth when it came to them." It is followed by the statement that they are not unique in misguidance, for nations before them also denied. He mentioned the most famous of them in the world and the most famous among the Arabs. The people of Noah were the first people to deny their messenger; Pharaoh denied Moses; and the people of Lot denied him. These are well known among the People of the Book. As for the companions of the Rass, 'Ad, Thamud, the companions of the Thicket and the people of Tubba', they are from the Arabs.

They are mentioned here right after the people of Noah because of the imaginary (khayali) association between the two peoples, which is an association of opposites (jami' al-tadadd), since their punishment was the opposite of the punishment of the people of Noah: their punishment was by being swallowed up by the earth, while the punishment of the people of Noah was by drowning. Then He mentioned Thamud because of the resemblance of their punishment to the punishment of the companions of the Rass, since their punishment was by the quaking of the earth and the thunderbolts of the sky, and because the companions of the Rass were remnants of Thamud. Then 'Ad was mentioned because their punishment came by an event in the atmosphere, namely the wind. Then Pharaoh and his people were mentioned because they denied the most famous of the messengers before Islam. The companions of the Thicket are the people of Shu'ayb, and they were allies of the Children of Israel.

He referred to the people of Lot as "the brothers of Lot," although they were not of his tribe. So the meaning of "brothers" is that they were closely attached to him. They were the people of Sodom, 'Amurah and their villages. Lot lived in Sodom, but he was not of their lineage, because the people of Sodom were Canaanites and Lot was a Hebrew. His saying the Exalted, "When their brother Lot said to them," [al-Shu'ara': 161] has already been mentioned in Surat al-Shu'ara'. The people of Tubba' are mentioned; they are the people of Yemen, and the Arabs did not count them as Arabs.

These nations were struck by a severe punishment in this world as a retribution for their denial of the messengers. The purpose is to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and to allude with a threat to his people who deny him, that what befell those (nations) may befall them.

Al-Rass: it is used as a noun for a well that is not lined with stone, and it is used as a verbal noun for burying and concealing. The exegetes differed concerning what is meant by it here.

The companions of the Rass are a people known by their attribution to al-Rass. It is possible that their attribution to al-Rass is the attribution of a thing to its location, like "the companions of the Thicket," "the companions of al-Hijr," and "the companions of the town." It is also possible that it is an attribution to an event that befell them, like "the companions of the Trench." Regarding the identification of the companions of the Rass there are eight or nine opinions, some of which overlap.

The discussion of them has already appeared in Surat al-Furqan. The more apparent view is that the attribution of "companions" to al-Rass is the attribution of a name to an event that occurred in it. It has been said that the companions of the Rass were punished by being swallowed up in the earth, so they fell into something like a well. It has also been said that it is a well into which its people threw Handhalah ibn Safwan, the messenger of a messenger of Allah sent to them, while he was alive; so it is then a name by dominance. It has also been said that it is (Falaj) in the land of al-Yamamah.

The discussion of the companions of the Rass has already appeared in Surat al-Furqan at His saying: "and 'Ad and Thamud and the companions of the Rass" [al-Furqan: 38].

The companions of the Thicket are of the people of Shu'ayb, and this has already appeared in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

The people of Tubba' are Himyar, of the Arabs of Yemen, and their mention has already appeared in Surat al-Dukhan.

The clause "each one denied the messengers" is a confirmation of the clause "Before them the people of Noah denied" to its end, which is why it is separated without a conjunction; and so that His saying "so My warning came true" may be built upon it, making it a threat that the warning will come true against them as it came true against those, arranged with the fa' upon their denial of the messengers. In this there is an honouring of the Prophet (ﷺ) and of the earlier messengers.

The tanwin of "kull" is the tanwin of compensation for the omitted genitive, i.e., "kullu ulaika" (all of those).

"Haqqa" means it was true and came to pass.

Al-wa'id: the warning of punishment. The reporting of it with "haqqa" requires that Allah threatened them with it, but they paid no heed and denied its occurrence, so it came true and was confirmed.

The ya' of the first person to which "wa'id" is attached has been omitted for the sake of rhyme (ri'ayah li al-fasilah), and this is common.

As for the companions of the Rass, 'Ad, Thamud, the companions of the Thicket and the people of Tubba', they are from the Arabs.

They are mentioned here right after the people of Noah because of the imaginary (khayali) association between the two peoples, which is an association of opposites (jami' al-tadadd), since their punishment was the opposite of the punishment of the people of Noah: their punishment was by being swallowed up by the earth, while the punishment of the people of Noah was by drowning. Then He mentioned Thamud because of the resemblance of their punishment to the punishment of the companions of the Rass, since their punishment was by the quaking of the earth and the thunderbolts of the sky, and because the companions of the Rass were remnants of Thamud. Then 'Ad was mentioned because their punishment came by an event in the atmosphere, namely the wind. Then Pharaoh and his people were mentioned because they denied the most famous of the messengers before Islam. The companions of the Thicket are the people of Shu'ayb, and they were allies of the Children of Israel.

He referred to the people of Lot as "the brothers of Lot," although they were not of his tribe. So the meaning of "brothers" is that they were closely attached to him. They were the people of Sodom, 'Amurah and their villages. Lot lived in Sodom, but he was not of their lineage, because the people of Sodom were Canaanites and Lot was a Hebrew. His saying the Exalted, "When their brother Lot said to them," [al-Shu'ara': 161] has already been mentioned in Surat al-Shu'ara'. The people of Tubba' are mentioned; they are the people of Yemen, and the Arabs did not count them as Arabs.

These nations were struck by a severe punishment in this world as a retribution for their denial of the messengers. The purpose is to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and to allude with a threat to his people who deny him, that what befell those (nations) may befall them.

Al-Rass: it is used as a noun for a well that is not lined with stone, and it is used as a verbal noun for burying and concealing. The exegetes differed concerning what is meant by it here.

The companions of the Rass are a people known by their attribution to al-Rass. It is possible that their attribution to al-Rass is the attribution of a thing to its location, like "the companions of the Thicket," "the companions of al-Hijr," and "the companions of the town." It is also possible that it is an attribution to an event that befell them, like "the companions of the Trench." Regarding the identification of the companions of the Rass there are eight or nine opinions, some of which overlap.

The discussion of them has already appeared in Surat al-Furqan. The more apparent view is that the attribution of "companions" to al-Rass is the attribution of a name to an event that occurred in it. It has been said that the companions of the Rass were punished by being swallowed up in the earth, so they fell into something like a well. It has also been said that it is a well into which its people threw Handhalah ibn Safwan, the messenger of a messenger of Allah sent to them, while he was alive; so it is then a name by dominance. It has also been said that it is (Falaj) in the land of al-Yamamah.

The discussion of the companions of the Rass has already appeared in Surat al-Furqan at His saying: "and 'Ad and Thamud and the companions of the Rass" [al-Furqan: 38].

The companions of the Thicket are of the people of Shu'ayb, and this has already appeared in Surat al-Shu'ara'.

The people of Tubba' are Himyar, of the Arabs of Yemen, and their mention has already appeared in Surat al-Dukhan.

The clause "each one denied the messengers" is a confirmation of the clause "Before them the people of Noah denied" to its end, which is why it is separated without a conjunction; and so that His saying "so My warning came true" may be built upon it, making it a threat that the warning will come true against them as it came true against those, arranged with the fa' upon their denial of the messengers. In this there is an honouring of the Prophet (ﷺ) and of the earlier messengers.

The tanwin of "kull" is the tanwin of compensation for the omitted genitive, i.e., "kullu ulaika" (all of those).

"Haqqa" means it was true and came to pass.

Al-wa'id: the warning of punishment. The reporting of it with "haqqa" requires that Allah threatened them with it, but they paid no heed and denied its occurrence, so it came true and was confirmed.

The ya' of the first person to which "wa'id" is attached has been omitted for the sake of rhyme (ri'ayah li al-fasilah), and this is common.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 50, verse 15:

﴿Did We then tire of the first creation? Nay, but they are in confusion about a new creation.﴾

The fa' of consequence (fa' al-tafri') indicates that this statement is a consequence of what precedes it, namely the sentence "Have they not looked at the sky above them, how We built it..." and His saying "as an insight and a reminder" (tabsiratan wa dhikra), which implicitly censures them for not gaining insight from it and not taking heed. And His saying "﴿So We caused to grow thereby gardens﴾ [Qaf: 9]" and His saying "and We revived thereby a dead land; thus will be the emergence (al-khurug)."

It may also be considered a consequence of His saying "﴿Thus will be the emergence﴾ [Qaf: 11]."

The interrogation introduced by the fa' is an interrogation of denial and rebuke, because they cannot but acknowledge that God did not tire of the first creation, since no rational person denies the perfection of the Creator's power and the absence of His incapacity.

"'Iyina" means "we were incapable." The verb 'ayya, when no pronoun is attached to it, is said in the assimilated form (mudghaman), which is the more common, and it is also said 'ayiya with the separated form (bi'l-fakk); when a pronoun is attached to it, the separated form becomes obligatory. Its meaning is: he was incapable of perfecting an action and was not guided to its method. It takes the preposition bi- (with), as one says 'ayiya bi'l-amr, where the bi- indicates transitivity (lil-mujawaza). As for a'ya with the hamza at its beginning, used intransitively, it means fatigue from walking or carrying a load, and it is an intransitive verb that does not take bi-.

Thus the meaning is: We were not incapable of the first creation of man, so how would We be incapable of re-creating him?

The "bal" in His saying "﴿Nay, but they are in confusion about a new creation﴾" is for idrab ibtali (a retractive transition) from the matter questioned, i.e., "Nay, We were not incapable of the first creation," meaning: while they know this, and they know that the first creation of things is greater than re-creating the dead, but the intense confusion has taken hold of them, and it has veiled their perception from the signs of possibility, so they deemed it impossible. Thus the idrab remains on its original basis of nullification.

Al-labs (confusion): mixing things of differing realities in such a way that it becomes difficult or impossible to distinguish their differing parts from one another.

What is meant by it is the confusion of the familiar and habitual, which they know of no other, with the rational necessity that cannot be negated. For the revival of the dead was confused for them with what is impossible in reason, so they affirmed the negation of its possibility and denied it, and they abandoned the analogy that whoever is able to originate what did not exist is even more able to restore what once existed.

The nominal sentence in His saying "﴿they are in confusion﴾" is used to indicate the permanence of this judgment upon them, that it is firmly rooted in their souls and never leaves them, and to allow the introduction of the particle of place in the predicate, which indicates their immersion in this confusion and its encompassing them like a container encompassing what it contains.

The min in His saying "﴿about a new creation﴾" is ibtida'iyya (of origin), and it is an attribute of "labs" (confusion), meaning a confusion that reaches them and results from a new creation, i.e., a confusion from disbelief in it.

The indefiniteness of "labs" is for the sense of kind (nau'iyya), and the indefiniteness of "khalq jadid" is likewise, meaning it is nothing but a creation among what occurs of God's creation of things, which He has directed toward its denial. For its indefiniteness the attribute "jadid" (new) is applied to it.

Al-jadid is the thing that is in the first times of its existence.

In this description there is a reproach against them and a ridicule of them for their deeming the resurrection impossible, meaning: make it a new creation like the first creation, and what difference is there between them?

In naming the restoration of people as "creation" for the resurrection there is an indication that it is a re-creation after the non-existence of the parts, not a gathering of their scattered pieces; and this has already been discussed at the beginning of the surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 50, verse 16:

Page 299
﴿And We have certainly created man, and We know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than his jugular vein.﴾
This is a detailed explanation of part of the first creation, by mentioning the creation of man, which is more important in this context, to draw attention to the fact that he is the intended meaning of the first creation, and so that what follows may be built upon it: ﴿and We know what his soul whispers to him﴾, which is a completion of the comprehensiveness of the attribute of knowledge in His saying: ﴿We already know what the earth diminishes of them﴾ [Qaf: 4], and so that the warning moves to the reckoning of people's deeds upon it, which is what He elaborated upon from His saying: ﴿when the two receivers receive﴾ [Qaf: 17], and so on.

He described the resurrection in terms of recompense, from His saying: ﴿and the Trumpet is blown﴾ [Qaf: 20] to His saying: ﴿and with Us is more﴾ [Qaf: 35].

The emphasis of this statement with the lam and "qad" takes into account the coordinated clauses, and these are: ﴿We know what his soul whispers to him﴾, because even though they knew that Allah created people, they did not know that Allah is Knowing of their states.

The word ﴿al-insan﴾ (man) encompasses all people, but the primary intended target is the polytheists, because they are the ones to whom this statement is directed. It is an indirect warning, as indicated by His saying after it: ﴿This is what you were trying to avoid﴾ [Qaf: 19], His saying: ﴿You were certainly heedless of this﴾ [Qaf: 22], and His saying: ﴿This is the Day of the Threat﴾ [Qaf: 20].

The ba' in His saying (bihi, "with it") is extra (za'ida) for emphasizing attachment, and the pronoun refers back to the relative clause, as if it were said: "what his soul speaks of," in the manner of "wa-msahu bi-ru'usikum" (and wipe over your heads).

The benefit of the statement that Allah knows what the soul of every human whispers is to draw attention to the breadth of Allah the Exalted's knowledge of all their states. If He knows the discourse of the soul, then it is no wonder that He knows what the earth diminishes of them.

The report about the act of creation is in the past tense, which is evident. As for the report about the knowledge of what the soul whispers, it is in the present tense, to indicate that the connection of His knowledge, Exalted is He, to the whispering is renewed, not ended nor limited, to establish the generality of Allah the Exalted's knowledge; and it is a metaphor (kinaya) for warning against harboring what does not please Allah.

Page 300
The clause ﴿and We are closer to him than his jugular vein﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "na'lamu" (We know).
Its purpose is to emphasize its governing verb and to confirm the continuity of knowledge of a person's inner self. The meaning of "tuwaswisu" is to speak in a hidden, whispered voice. Its verbal noun is al-waswas and al-waswasa, and it is used here metaphorically for what roams in the soul of thoughts, estimations and resolutions, because whispering is the closest thing to which those thoughts are likened and the best thing borrowed for them, since it combines the various states of what roams in the mind of estimations; and other terms such as tawahhum (imagining) and tafakkur (reflecting) only indicate some states of thoughts and not others.

Al-habl (the vein/cord) here is one of the "cords" (hibal) of the body. These are the thick vessels known in medicine as the arteries (al-shara'in), whose singular is shiryan, with the shin unpointed and vowelled with fatha or kasra, and with the ra' sukun; they are known as the pulsing vessels (al-'uruq al-dawarib), and their origin is from the left chamber of the two chambers of the heart. The arteries have much function in the life of the body, because they are what carry blood from the heart to the most important principal organs, such as the lungs, the brain, the spinal cord, the two kidneys, the stomach and the intestines. The arteries have names according to their destinations among the principal organs.

Al-warid (the jugular): it is one of the arteries, and it is the second of two arteries that emerge from the left chamber of the heart. In medical science its name is aorta (awrutiyy), and it branches into three branches, the third of which divides into two parts, a larger part and a smaller part. From this smaller part come out two arteries called the carotid (al-subatiyy), which ascend to the right and left alongside the jugular veins (al-wadajayn), and all these divisions are called al-warid. In the body there are two jugulars, which are two vessels flanking the two sides of the neck at its front, connected to the aorta (al-watin), coming to it from the head.

The names of its parts may differ according to their positions in the body: in the neck it is called al-warid, in the heart it is called al-watin, in the back it is called al-abhar, and in the arm and thigh they call it al-akhal and al-nasa, and in the little finger it is called al-aslam.

The genitive construction "habl" to "warid" is explicative (bayaniyya), meaning the cord which is the jugular, for when a more general term is annexed to a more specific one in speech, it is an explicative annexation, as in their saying: "shajar al-arak" (the tree of the arak).

Page 301
Nearness here is a metaphor (kinaya) for the encompassing of knowledge of the state, because nearness entails awareness; and it is not nearness in place, by the evidence of observation. So the statement comes to be a eloquent simile, the likening of an intelligible to a perceptible, and this is from building a simile upon a metonymy, in the position of building a metaphor upon a metaphor.
Among the subtleties of this illustration is that the jugular vein, despite its nearness, a person does not feel its nearness because of its concealment; and likewise God's nearness to a person through His knowledge is a nearness that a person does not perceive. Therefore the likeness of this nearness to the nearness of the jugular vein was chosen. By this, this simile surpassed every simile of its kind in expressing the state of nearness that occurs in the speech of the eloquent, like their saying: "he is from him the seat of the midwife and the knot of the waistcloth," and the saying of Zuhayr:

"They, and the valley of al-Rass, are like the hand to the mouth."

And the saying of Handhala ibn Sayyar, who is Handhala ibn Tha'laba ibn Sayyar al-'Ijli, a mukhadram poet:

"Every man who rises in the morning among his family, while death is nearer than the strap of his sandal."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 50, verses 17–18:

﴿When the two receivers receive, one seated on the right and one on the left.﴾ ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is with him an observer ready.﴾

(Idh) is connected to the word "aqrab" (nearer), because the superlative (ism al-tafdil) may govern an adverbial complement (zarf), even though it does not govern the subject or the direct object. The language is more liberal with adverbs and prepositional phrases than with other elements, and this is a well-known, established rule. The passage serves as a transition (takhallus) to admonition and to the threat of recompense on the Day of Resurrection, and to the recompense arising from the reckoning of deeds, both good and bad, which is known from many verses of the Qur'an. This transition by means of the word (idh), which denotes time, is among the most graceful of transitions.

The definiteness of "al-mutalaqqiyan" (the two receivers) is either definiteness of reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), if the verse was revealed after verses that mention the guardian angels (al-hafaza), or definiteness of the genus (ta'rif al-jins). The dual form here indicates that this genus is divided into pairs.

Talaqqi (receiving) means taking a thing from the hand of the one who gives it. It is used metaphorically for the recording of statements and deeds at the moment they proceed from people.

The object of yatalaqqa (receives) is omitted, being indicated by his words: ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is with him an observer ready﴾, since their statements and actions are recorded.

From the verse it is deduced that every person has two angels who record his deeds, one on his right and the other on his left. It has been reported in the Sunnah, through acceptable chains of transmission, that the one on the right records the good deeds and the one on the left records the bad deeds. It has also been reported that they accompany the person from the time he becomes accountable until he dies.

His words ﴿one seated on the right and one on the left﴾ may be understood as "qa'id" (seated) being a substitute (badal) for "al-mutalaqqiyan," as a partial substitute (badal ba'd), with "on the right" connected to "qa'id." It is placed before its complement for emphasis on what it indicates of encompassing both sides, and for the sake of the rhyme (fasila).

It is also possible that "on the right" is a fronted predicate (khabar muqaddam), and "qa'id" is the subject (mubtada'), and the sentence serves as an explanation (bayan) of the sentence "the two receivers receive."

His words "and on the left" are conjoined to the clause "receive" and are not conjoined to his words "on the right," because the meaning is not that one seated person is seated on both sides; rather, each of the two sides has its own independent seated one. The implied sense is: on the right is a seated one, and on the left is another seated one.

The definiteness in "al-yamin" (the right) and "al-shimal" (the left) is definiteness of reference, or the article is a substitute for the omitted genitive, i.e., on the right of the human being and on his left.

Qa'id means one who sits, like jalis for one who sits with another, akil for one who eats with another, sharib for one who drinks with another, and khalit for one who mixes with another. The usual pattern of fa'il is that it means either the doer (fa'il) or the done-to (maf'ul). Since the form of mufa'ala carries both the sense of the doer and of the one done to together, it is permissible for fa'il to come from it in either sense, relying on context. For this reason they said of a man's wife, "qa'idatuhu."

Qa'id is used figuratively for the constant companion who never leaves him, just as they applied qa'id to the guardian, because he is constantly with the thing entrusted to his protection.

The clause ﴿not a word does he utter﴾ etc. is an explanation (mabniyya) of the clause "the two receivers receive," and therefore it is separated from it. "Ma" is negative, and the pronoun in "yalfizu" refers to the human being.

Lafz (utterance) is pronouncing a word that indicates a meaning, even if only part of a meaning, unlike qawl (statement), which is speech that conveys a complete meaning.

"Min" is redundant in the object of the negated verb, to make explicit the generality. The exception in his words ﴿except that there is with him an observer ready﴾ is an exception from general circumstances, meaning: he utters no statement in any state except in the state in which there is with him an observer ready.

The more apparent view is that this generality is intended as specificity, by the indication of his words ﴿except that there is with him an observer ready﴾, because the watching here relates to what is in the statements of good or evil, so that the recompense may be based upon it. The guardians therefore record only what bears on the person's well-being or corruption, since there is no wisdom in recording other than what the recompense depends upon. Thus said Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. Al-Hasan said: they record everything that issues from the servant. Mujahid and Abu al-Jawza' said: even his groaning during his illness. The same is related from Malik ibn Anas.

The word "qawl" was singled out for mention because the primary intent of this warning is the polytheists, who were held accountable for their statements that indicate polytheism, or for their rejection of the Prophet ﷺ, or for harming him, and they were not held accountable for their deeds, since they were not under obligation to perform deeds while in a state of associating partners with God.

As for deeds that are a consequence of polytheism, such as circumambulating an idol, or a consequence of harming the Prophet ﷺ, such as throwing the entrails of a camel upon him during his prayer, and the like, they are held accountable for these within their statements, since those actions are never free from accompanying statements for which they are held accountable in proportion to what accompanied them.

And because among evil statements are some that have a strong effect in misguidance, such as calling to the worship of idols, forbidding people from following the truth, promoting falsehood by casting doubts, and deceiving the naive, and the like. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Will people be thrown into the Fire on their faces except for the harvest of their tongues?" It is known by necessary implication (dalalat al-iqtida') that being held accountable for deeds is more fitting than being held accountable for statements, and that indication is sufficient to remind the believers.

His words ﴿except that there is with him an observer ready﴾ form a clause in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The pronoun in "ladayhi" refers to the human being, and the meaning is: at the utterance of his statement.

"Ateed" is an adjective of the pattern fa'il from "atada," meaning "prepared," and the "ta'" is substituted for the first "dal," since its origin is "adid," meaning prepared, as in His saying: ﴿And she prepared for them a couch﴾ [Yusuf: 31].

In my view, "ateed" here is an attributive adjective (sifa mushabbaha) from the expression "ataduh," with a "damma" on the "ta'," when a thing becomes large and bulky, as a metaphor for being strong. By this, a difference arises between it and his later words ﴿This is what is with me, ready﴾ [Qaf: 23], and the perfect paronomasia (jinas tamm) between the two words is obtained.

The exegetes have agreed upon interpreting "talaqqi" in his words "al-mutalaqqiyan" as the receiving of deeds for the purpose of recording them in the scrolls to bring them forth for reckoning. This interpretation hovers around making the omitted object of "yatalaqqa" what is indicated by his following words ﴿not a word does he utter but there is with him an observer ready﴾, by its apparent indication or by necessary implication. So their estimate is: when the two receivers receive the human being's deed and his statement. On their reading, this sentence is separate from the clause ﴿and the agony of death has come with truth﴾ [Qaf: 19], as we shall explain.

Fakhr al-Din has a subtle meaning. After summarizing the interpretation of the verse in a way that accords with the majority view, he said: It may be said that "talaqqi" means "meeting," as one says: so-and-so received the caravan. On this reading, its meaning is: at the time they meet him, one is on his right and one on his left, seated. So the two receivers in this reading are the two angels who take his soul from the Angel of Death: one takes the souls of the righteous and conveys them to joy, and the other takes the souls of the wicked and conveys them to woe and destruction until the Day of Resurrection, that is, at the time of their meeting and their questioning him as to which of the two groups he belongs. There is a seated one on the right and a seated one on the left, two angels who descend, and with him are two other angels, scribes of his deeds. What we have mentioned is supported by His saying: ﴿a driver and a witness﴾ [Qaf: 21]. The witness is the seated one, and the driver is the receiver who receives his soul from the Angel of Death and drives him to his abode at the time of the return. This is the more known of the two views and closer to understanding. End of quotation.

It seems he inclines toward the interpretation of His saying: ﴿Why then, when it [the soul] reaches the throat, and you at that time are looking on, and We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 83–85]. We do not hesitate about the soundness of this interpretation except regarding the established existence of two angels who take over the dead person's soul from the hand of the Angel of Death at its taking and place it in the abode suitable to its state. It is presumed of Fakhr al-Din that he was informed of this. It may be supported by what al-Qurtubi mentioned in al-Tadhkira from the Musnad of al-Tayalisi, on the authority of al-Bara', and from the Sunan of al-Nasa'i, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "When the believing dead person is present, angels of mercy come to him with a white silk cloth, saying: 'Come out, O soul, content and pleasing [to God], to rest and sweet fragrance and a Lord who is pleased, not angry.' When the Angel takes it, he does not leave it in his hand for an instant, and it comes out like the finest musk scent, and the angels carry it upward until they bring it to the gate of heaven." He related the hadith in full, except that in the hadith it is "angels" in plural, while in the verse it is "the two receivers" in the dual.

On this interpretation, the object of "yatalaqqa" is what is indicated by his following words ﴿and the agony of death has come﴾ [Qaf: 19]. The estimate is: when the two receivers receive the human being's soul. "Al-yamin" and "al-shimal" in his words ﴿on the right and on the left﴾ are definite as a substitute for the genitive, i.e., on its right and on its left, a seated one, and this is by distribution: on the right of one of them and on the left of the other. "Qa'id" is used in the sense of "two seated ones," since fa'il in the sense of fa'il may be treated as fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, as in the saying of al-Azraq ibn Tarafah:

He shot me with a matter from which I, and my father, were innocent, and out of the well he shot me.

Limiting the statement to "not a word does he utter" at that time is evident, because in that state a person cannot perform actions due to his incapacity, so in general only statements issue from him, such as complaints, groans, or testimony to the Oneness of God, or their opposite, and among these are bequests and acknowledgments.
