Since the form of mufa'ala carries both the sense of the doer and of the one done to together, it is permissible for fa'il to come from it in either sense, relying on context. For this reason they said of a man's wife, "qa'idatuhu."

Qa'id is used figuratively for the constant companion who never leaves him, just as they applied qa'id to the guardian, because he is constantly with the thing entrusted to his protection.

The clause ﴿not a word does he utter﴾ etc. is an explanation (mabniyya) of the clause "the two receivers receive," and therefore it is separated from it. "Ma" is negative, and the pronoun in "yalfizu" refers to the human being.

Lafz (utterance) is pronouncing a word that indicates a meaning, even if only part of a meaning, unlike qawl (statement), which is speech that conveys a complete meaning.

"Min" is redundant in the object of the negated verb, to make explicit the generality. The exception in his words ﴿except that there is with him an observer ready﴾ is an exception from general circumstances, meaning: he utters no statement in any state except in the state in which there is with him an observer ready.

The more apparent view is that this generality is intended as specificity, by the indication of his words ﴿except that there is with him an observer ready﴾, because the watching here relates to what is in the statements of good or evil, so that the recompense may be based upon it. The guardians therefore record only what bears on the person's well-being or corruption, since there is no wisdom in recording other than what the recompense depends upon. Thus said Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah. Al-Hasan said: they record everything that issues from the servant. Mujahid and Abu al-Jawza' said: even his groaning during his illness. The same is related from Malik ibn Anas.

The word "qawl" was singled out for mention because the primary intent of this warning is the polytheists, who were held accountable for their statements that indicate polytheism, or for their rejection of the Prophet ﷺ, or for harming him, and they were not held accountable for their deeds, since they were not under obligation to perform deeds while in a state of associating partners with God.

As for deeds that are a consequence of polytheism, such as circumambulating an idol, or a consequence of harming the Prophet ﷺ, such as throwing the entrails of a camel upon him during his prayer, and the like, they are held accountable for these within their statements, since those actions are never free from accompanying statements for which they are held accountable in proportion to what accompanied them.

And because among evil statements are some that have a strong effect in misguidance, such as calling to the worship of idols, forbidding people from following the truth, promoting falsehood by casting doubts, and deceiving the naive, and the like. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Will people be thrown into the Fire on their faces except for the harvest of their tongues?" It is known by necessary implication (dalalat al-iqtida') that being held accountable for deeds is more fitting than being held accountable for statements, and that indication is sufficient to remind the believers.

His words ﴿except that there is with him an observer ready﴾ form a clause in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). The pronoun in "ladayhi" refers to the human being, and the meaning is: at the utterance of his statement.

"Ateed" is an adjective of the pattern fa'il from "atada," meaning "prepared," and the "ta'" is substituted for the first "dal," since its origin is "adid," meaning prepared, as in His saying: ﴿And she prepared for them a couch﴾ [Yusuf: 31].

In my view, "ateed" here is an attributive adjective (sifa mushabbaha) from the expression "ataduh," with a "damma" on the "ta'," when a thing becomes large and bulky, as a metaphor for being strong. By this, a difference arises between it and his later words ﴿This is what is with me, ready﴾ [Qaf: 23], and the perfect paronomasia (jinas tamm) between the two words is obtained.

The exegetes have agreed upon interpreting "talaqqi" in his words "al-mutalaqqiyan" as the receiving of deeds for the purpose of recording them in the scrolls to bring them forth for reckoning. This interpretation hovers around making the omitted object of "yatalaqqa" what is indicated by his following words ﴿not a word does he utter but there is with him an observer ready﴾, by its apparent indication or by necessary implication. So their estimate is: when the two receivers receive the human being's deed and his statement. On their reading, this sentence is separate from the clause ﴿and the agony of death has come with truth﴾ [Qaf: 19], as we shall explain.

Fakhr al-Din has a subtle meaning. After summarizing the interpretation of the verse in a way that accords with the majority view, he said: It may be said that "talaqqi" means "meeting," as one says: so-and-so received the caravan. On this reading, its meaning is: at the time they meet him, one is on his right and one on his left, seated. So the two receivers in this reading are the two angels who take his soul from the Angel of Death: one takes the souls of the righteous and conveys them to joy, and the other takes the souls of the wicked and conveys them to woe and destruction until the Day of Resurrection, that is, at the time of their meeting and their questioning him as to which of the two groups he belongs. There is a seated one on the right and a seated one on the left, two angels who descend, and with him are two other angels, scribes of his deeds. What we have mentioned is supported by His saying: ﴿a driver and a witness﴾ [Qaf: 21]. The witness is the seated one, and the driver is the receiver who receives his soul from the Angel of Death and drives him to his abode at the time of the return. This is the more known of the two views and closer to understanding. End of quotation.

It seems he inclines toward the interpretation of His saying: ﴿Why then, when it [the soul] reaches the throat, and you at that time are looking on, and We are nearer to him than you, but you do not see﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 83–85]. We do not hesitate about the soundness of this interpretation except regarding the established existence of two angels who take over the dead person's soul from the hand of the Angel of Death at its taking and place it in the abode suitable to its state. It is presumed of Fakhr al-Din that he was informed of this. It may be supported by what al-Qurtubi mentioned in al-Tadhkira from the Musnad of al-Tayalisi, on the authority of al-Bara', and from the Sunan of al-Nasa'i, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "When the believing dead person is present, angels of mercy come to him with a white silk cloth, saying: 'Come out, O soul, content and pleasing [to God], to rest and sweet fragrance and a Lord who is pleased, not angry.' When the Angel takes it, he does not leave it in his hand for an instant, and it comes out like the finest musk scent, and the angels carry it upward until they bring it to the gate of heaven." He related the hadith in full, except that in the hadith it is "angels" in plural, while in the verse it is "the two receivers" in the dual.

On this interpretation, the object of "yatalaqqa" is what is indicated by his following words ﴿and the agony of death has come﴾ [Qaf: 19]. The estimate is: when the two receivers receive the human being's soul. "Al-yamin" and "al-shimal" in his words ﴿on the right and on the left﴾ are definite as a substitute for the genitive, i.e., on its right and on its left, a seated one, and this is by distribution: on the right of one of them and on the left of the other. "Qa'id" is used in the sense of "two seated ones," since fa'il in the sense of fa'il may be treated as fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, as in the saying of al-Azraq ibn Tarafah:

He shot me with a matter from which I, and my father, were innocent, and out of the well he shot me.

Limiting the statement to "not a word does he utter" at that time is evident, because in that state a person cannot perform actions due to his incapacity, so in general only statements issue from him, such as complaints, groans, or testimony to the Oneness of God, or their opposite, and among these are bequests and acknowledgments.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 50, verse 19:

﴿And the intoxication of death will come with the truth. That is what you were trying to avoid.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) with the clause ﴿And We are closer to him than the jugular vein﴾ [Qaf: 16], because both share the warning of recompense for deeds. This is a progression through the stages of the matters that befall a person, which move him from one state to another until he reaches the recompense for his deeds, which the two recorders (al-Hafizan) have counted.

The expression in the conjoined clause was shifted to the past tense rather than the present tense used in the clause it is conjoined to, because, due to its imminence, it has become as though it has already occurred, intentionally, to instill terror into the souls of the polytheists, as is understood from His words: ﴿That is what you were trying to avoid﴾, similar to the saying of God Most High: ﴿Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 8].

According to the view that al-Fakhr (al-Razi) preferred in his commentary on ﴿When the two receivers receive﴾ [Qaf: 17] and what follows, the clauses ﴿And the intoxication of death will come...﴾ etc. may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

The meaning would be: "And the intoxication of death has come with the truth at that time."

The verb "come" (majiʾ) is a metaphor for occurrence and befalling, and in this metaphor there is an expression of the magnitude of the state of a person's dying and his awareness that he is departing from the life to which he became accustomed and to which his heart was attached.

The word "sakrah" (intoxication) is a noun for what befalls a person of pain or disturbance of temperament that veils the perception of the intellect, so that perception is disordered and the intellect is overcome by unconsciousness. It is derived from "al-sakr" (with a fatha and then a sukun), which means closing, because it closes the intellect; from it comes the description "sakran" (intoxicated).

The "bi" in His words "bi-al-haqq" (with the truth) denotes association (mulabasa). It may be a circumstantial clause (hal) of "intoxication of death," meaning characterized as being truth, where "al-haqq" is that which is established and confirmed so that it does not fail, that is, the intoxication after which there is no hope of prolonging life. Or it may be a circumstantial clause of "death," meaning associated with being the truth, that is, the decreed and written matter upon people, so they are bound by it; or the seriousness that is the opposite of frivolity, as in His words: ﴿He created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾ [al-An'am: 73], together with His words: ﴿And We did not create the heaven and the earth and what is between them in vain﴾ [Sad: 27].

The phrase "dhalika" (that) is a reference to death, by treating its imminent occurrence as though it were already present and witnessed.

"Tahid" means to flee and run away, and it is used metaphorically for aversion or for avoiding the causes of death. The address is to the intended human being, and primarily to those intended, namely the polytheists, because they are most averse to death, since their life is purely material, so they want a long life. God Most High said: ﴿And among those who associated partners [with God] is one who wishes he could be given a life of a thousand years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 96], since they have no hope in another life and no hope of attaining its bliss. As for the believers, their aversion to death, which is rooted in human nature to the degree of familiarity, does not reach the point of distress from it. In the hadith: "Whoever loves to meet God, God loves to meet him, and whoever dislikes to meet God, God dislikes to meet him," and its interpretation is that the believer loves to meet God out of hope for reward, and the disbeliever dislikes meeting God. The Prophet (ﷺ) explained it, saying: "Indeed, when death attends the believer, he sees what God has prepared for him of good, so he loves to meet God," that is, the disbeliever is the opposite. God Most High also said, addressing the Jews: ﴿Say: Indeed, the death from which you flee will surely meet you﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 8].

The placing of "minhu" (from it) before "tahid" is for emphasis on that from which the aversion is, and for the sake of harmony with the verse-ending (fasilah).

The trumpet will be blown; that is the Day of the Threat. ﴿And the trumpet will be blown; that is the Day of the Threat.﴾ And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness.

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon ﴿And the agony of death will come with truth﴾ [Qaf: 19], according to the interpretation of the majority (al-Jumhur). As for the interpretation of al-Fakhr (al-Razi), the sentence is resumed (mustaʾnafa), and the past tense in His words "wa-nufikha" (and it was blown) is used in the sense of the present, meaning: it is blown into the trumpet; the past form is used for it because its occurrence is certain, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The command of Allah has come, so do not seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Nahl: 1]. The one indicated by "dhalika" (that) in His words ﴿that is the Day of the Threat﴾ is the time at which the trumpet is blown, for that time is the Day of the Threat.

As for the blowing into the trumpet (al-nafkh fi al-ṣūr), its discussion has already preceded at His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And His is the dominion on the day the trumpet is blown﴾ [al-Anʿam: 73], in Surat al-Anʿam.

The sentence ﴿that is the Day of the Threat﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ).

The demonstrative in His words ﴿that is the Day of the Threat﴾ refers to the benefit (al-nafʿ) derived from the verb ﴿And the trumpet will be blown﴾. The predication of the blowing as being "the Day of the Threat" is by way of an elided genitive (taqdir muḍāf), meaning: that is the arrival of the Day of the Threat.

The idafa (genitive construction) of "day" to "the Threat" is an idafa of a thing to that in which it occurs, meaning: the day on which the threat that they had been threatened with takes place. The restriction to mentioning the Threat is because, as you know, the primary intent of this verse is the polytheists. In the speech there is an ellipsis (ikhtiṣār), its implied meaning being: and the Day of the Promise (al-Waʿd).

The sentence "every soul came" (jāʾat kullu nafs) is conjoined (ʿuṭifat) to the sentence "the trumpet was blown." By "every soul" (kullu nafs) is meant every soul among those spoken of, namely the polytheists, and several matters indicate this:

The first: the context (al-siyāq).

The second: His saying "with it a driver" (maʿahā sāʾiq), because the driver fits the herding of the people of crimes; as for those guided to honour, they are led by a leader walking in front of them. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿as if they were being driven to death﴾ [al-Anfal: 6].

The third: His saying after it ﴿You were heedless of this﴾ [Qaf: 22].

The fourth: His saying after it ﴿And his companion will say, "This is what is ready with me"﴾ [Qaf: 23], and the verse.

The sentence ﴿with it a driver and a witness﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the sentence "every soul came." "Sāʾiq" (driver) is in the nominative by the adverbial phrase "maʿahā" (with it), according to the opinion of the one who permits this, or it is a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is "maʿahā." It is also permissible that the sentence ﴿maʿahā sāʾiq wa-shahīd﴾ be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "every soul." The conjunction of "wa-shahīd" (and witness) to "sāʾiq" may be a conjunction of one entity to another entity, in which case the meaning is two angels: one of them drives the soul to the place of gathering, and the other bears witness against it by what its records of deeds contain. It may also be a conjunction of attributes, as in the line:

To the king, the generous, and the son of the hero,

in which case he is one king.

The driver is one who places another before him, leading him in motion so that he remains within his sight lest he escape; and this is part of the manner of walking someone toward what is evil. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿as if they were being driven to death﴾ [al-Anfal: 6], and He said: ﴿And those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in groups﴾ [al-Zumar: 71]. As for His saying: ﴿And those who feared their Lord will be driven to Paradise in groups﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], it is an instance of stylistic correspondence (mushākala). The opposite of al-sawq (driving) is al-qawd (leading).

The clause of saying and what is said occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to every soul, or the position of a descriptive clause (*sifah*). The signs of address in the words "kunta" (you were), "anka" (from you), "ghita'aka" (your covering) and "basaruka" (your sight) are in the masculine singular, by way of *ta'wil* (reinterpretation, here taking the word *nafs*, soul, to mean the person or the human being). The masculine then prevailed over the feminine. This statement comes from God, Exalted is He, and it begins the mention of the reckoning.

*Al-ghaflah* is being absorbed in something that ought to be known. Here it is applied to denial and repudiation, by way of mockery. This is reinforced by His words, "So We removed from you your covering," meaning: We showed you the proof through the senses, so this too is mockery.

The phrase "in heedlessness" was chosen rather than saying "heedless" (*ghafilan*), to indicate that heedlessness had firmly taken hold of him. For this reason, the image of it is followed by the image of the covering.

The removal of the covering is a figure for the attainment of certainty about a thing after denying its occurrence. The meaning is: We removed from you the covering which was screening from you the occurrence of this day with all that it contains. The removal is attributed to God, Exalted is He, because He is the one who made apparent to him the causes of attaining certainty through the evidence of *ayn al-yaqin* (certainty by direct witnessing).

The "covering" is attributed to the pronoun of the addressed human being, to indicate that it is specific to him and that it is something by which he is known.

The sharpness of sight (*hiddat al-basar*) is the strength of its penetration into the thing seen. The sharpness of anything is the strength of its effect. From this comes the sharpness of the mind. The statement contains a comparison of the attainment of certainty with the seeing of a visible thing by a strong eye. Restricting it with the words "today" carries an implicit reproach: your condition today is not your condition before today, when you were in the world denying the resurrection.

The meaning is: you have now witnessed the resurrection, the gathering and the recompense, whereas they used to deny all of that. They said, "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be held to account?" and they said, "We shall not be punished." So he has now seen the punishment with his own eyes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 50, verse 23:

﴿And his companion will say, "This is what is ready with me."﴾

The waw here is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and the clause is a circumstantial phrase (hal) referring to the "you" (ta' al-khitab) in His words: ﴿Certainly you were in heedlessness of this﴾ [Qaf: 22].

That is: he is reproached at the sight of the punishment with the words ﴿Certainly you were in heedlessness of this﴾ [Qaf: 22], while his companion says ﴿This is what is ready with me.﴾

The pronoun of the third person in His words "his companion" (qarinuhu) refers either to every soul or to the human being.

"Qarin" is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, i.e., one who is joined to another (maqrun ila ghayrih). It seems that the verb qarana is derived from al-qaran (with a vowel on the first letter), which means a rope, and they used to tie a camel to another like it to carry the howdah; so qarin was borrowed for the constant companion. This is not an iltifat (shift of pronoun), since it is not a change of pronoun; rather it is a specification of the style of speech, and the third-person singular pronoun is referred back to it in consideration of the meaning of "nafs," i.e., person, or the masculine has prevailed over the feminine.

The demonstrative in His words "This is what is with me" etc. is explained by His words ﴿what is ready with me.﴾

The "ma" in His words "what is with me" is a relative pronoun (mawsula) in apposition to the demonstrative. "Ladayya" is a complement (silah), and "ataid" is the predicate of the demonstrative.

The exegetes differed concerning the intended meaning of "qarin" in this verse, according to three opinions. Qatadah, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Ibn Zayd, and Mujahid in one of his two statements said: it is the angel assigned to the human being who drives him to the place of gathering, i.e., he is the driver and witness. This requires that "qarin" in His later words ﴿His companion will say, "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress"﴾ [Qaf: 27] have a meaning other than the meaning of "qarin" in His words: ﴿And his companion will say, "This is what is ready with me."﴾

Also from Mujahid: the qarin is the devil of the disbeliever who used to adorn disbelief for him in the world, i.e., the one mentioned in His Exalted words: ﴿And We appointed for them companions who made attractive to them what was before them and what was behind them﴾ [Fussilat: 25].

Also from Ibn Zayd: his qarin is his companion from among mankind, i.e., the one who was his companion in the world.

Based on the difference over the meaning of "qarin," the interpretation of His words ﴿This is what is ready with me﴾ differs. If the qarin is the angel, the indication by His words "this" refers to the punishment assigned to that angel. If the qarin is a devil or a human, the indication is open to referring to the punishment as in the first view, or to refer back to the antecedent of the third-person pronoun in His words "qarinuhu," which is in the disbeliever himself, i.e., "this which is with me," so "ladayya" would mean "maʿi" (with me), since no one is free of a companion with whom he is at ease in conversation. The intended one is the companion of polytheism who is similar.

Allah has mentioned who was a companion of the believer from among the polytheists and the difference of their two states on the Day of Recompense in His words: ﴿A speaker among them will say, "Indeed, I had a companion who would say, 'Are you really among those who believe?'"﴾ [As-Saffat: 51], the verse in Surat as-Saffat. The statement of the qarin, ﴿This is what is ready with me,﴾ is used in the sense of anguish, regret and apprehension, because when he saw what the punishment was, he knew that it had been prepared for him; or, when he saw what his companion had sent ahead, he knew that he would follow in his footsteps, like the story of the two bulls, the white and the red, of which the lion sought help from the red one to eat the white bull; then the lion came after a day to eat the red bull, so the red one climbed a hillock and cried out: "Verily, I was eaten the day the white bull was eaten."

The meaning of "ataid" was mentioned at His words: ﴿except that with him is a watcher, ready﴾ [Qaf: 18], and here it is specifically the meaning which the exegetes explained, i.e., prepared and made ready.

Transition from addressing the soul to addressing the two angels appointed (over the person): the driver (al-sa'ik) and the witness (al-shahid). The speech is the object of an omitted verb of saying. The sentence is a fresh resumptive statement (isti'naf ibtida'i), a shift from addressing one group to addressing another. The dual form in His words "alqiya" (cast, both of you) may be used in its original sense, so the address is to the driver and the witness. It may also be used to address a single angel, the one appointed over Hell, and is addressed in the dual form following a usage current in speech, as people commonly say that a traveler is accompanied by two companions. This is a well-known manner, as Imru' al-Qays said:

Al-'anid: one who is intensely obstinate, i.e., one who persists in arrogance and resists the truth while knowing that he is in falsehood.

Among its examples is His words: ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have done and love to be praised for what they have not done - do not think them safe from punishment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 188]. Accordingly, "the one who set up another god with Allah" refers to the disbeliever whose plural is governed by "kull" (every). It applies to the group of disbelievers, so the object pronoun in "alqaynahu" (we cast him) is equivalent to a plural pronoun, meaning "fa-alqiyahum" (so cast them).

It is also permissible for the relative noun to be a subject (mubtada') in a resumed statement (istinaf al-kalam), with the relative clause implicitly containing the meaning of a conditional (shart). This is why the particle "fa" appears in its predicate, because of the conditional meaning within it. This usage is common. The purpose here is to emphasize the generality expressed in His words ﴿every stubborn disbeliever﴾ [Qaf: 24].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 50, verse 27:

﴿His companion will say: "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, but he was in far error."﴾

The relating of the companion's speech follows the usual manner in which exchanges are reported in the Qur'an, namely the style of disjunction (al-fasl), in which the verb of saying is not joined by a conjunction (ʿatf) to what precedes it. This is the same style that we mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Will You place therein one who will cause corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], in the commentary on Surah al-Baqarah. It indicates that in the context there is an unstated speech, which is the speech of the companion's companion, omitted for brevity. The evidence for it is what the companion's words contain of denying that he himself caused the other to transgress, when he said: ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, but he was in far error.﴾ This has been related explicitly in Surah Sad by His saying: ﴿This is a host rushing in with you. No welcome for them; indeed, they will burn in the Fire.﴾ [Sad: 59] ﴿They will say, "Rather, you—no welcome for you! You have brought this upon us, so wretched is the abode."﴾ [Sad: 60] ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, whoever brought this upon us, increase him in punishment doubled in the Fire."﴾ [Sad: 61]

The omitted content here is to be understood as follows: when the stubborn disbeliever arrived at the Fire, he wished to disown his disbelief and his obstinacy, and he cast the responsibility upon his companion who used to adorn disbelief for him, saying: "This companion made me transgress," and his companion replied: ﴿Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, but he was in far error.﴾

This companion is therefore the companion who was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And his companion will say, "This is what is ready with me."﴾ [Qaf: 23].

Page 314

At-Tughyan (transgression) is exceeding the limit in self-magnification, injustice, and disbelief. Its verb has both a ya' and a waw form: it is said ṭaghiya yaṭghā like raḍiya, and ṭaghā yaṭghū like daʿā.

So the meaning of "mā aṭghaytuhu" ("I did not make him transgress") is: I did not make him a transgressor, that is, I did not command him to transgress nor did I adorn it for him. The "istidrak" (corrective particle, "but") arises from the intensity of the comparison between him and his companion, especially if by "the companion" is meant his devil appointed over him, for he was joined to him from the time of his understanding. Thus the istidrak serves to dispel the assumption that their association requires that the transgression in him was due to the companion's inducing it; he negates that about himself. For this reason he followed the istidrak with the clause ﴿but he was in far error﴾, informing that his companion was already astray before, so that his association with him in being appointed to him or in companionship added nothing to his misguidance. This is similar to what God related of the two groups in His saying: ﴿When those who were followed disowned those who followed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 166]. The verb (kāna) serves to convey that error is established for him originally, inseparable from his constitution.

Al-Baʿid (far): it is used metaphorically for one who has reached, in the nature of his kind, a degree that intellect does not reach easily, just as the traveller's journey does not reach a distant place except with hardship; or it means distant in time, that is, ancient and rooted, in which case it is an emphasis on what is conveyed by the verb (kāna). It was discussed previously at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever associates others with God has strayed far astray﴾ [an-Nisa': 116], in Surah an-Nisa'.

The meaning: that the entrenchment of error in him indicates that he was not a follower of what others dictated to him, because the state of a follower in a matter is that he is not firmly established in it, like the knowledge of one who imitates (al-muqallid) and the knowledge of the speculative theologians (al-nuzzar).

[p. 315]

This is a report of a statement that will be made on that Day from the side of God, exalted is He, to the two groups: those who followed and those who were followed. The pronoun refers to something not mentioned in the speech but indicated by His words ﴿So We removed from you your covering﴾ (Qaf 50:22).

The verb "He said" is not joined by a conjunction (waw) to what precedes it because it occurs in the context of dialogue. The use of the past form indicates that its occurrence is certain. Thus the exchange takes place among three parties.

[p. 315 continues]

Al-ikhtisam means mukhasama (dispute), and it is a verbal noun of the ifti'al pattern. The original function of this pattern is to express the effect (muṭāwaʿa) of certain verbs, but it has come to be used for reciprocity, like ijtawaru, i'tawaru and ikhtasamu.

The prohibition of disputing among themselves implies that the disbelieving souls claimed that their companions had led them into transgression, that the companions disavowed this, and that the souls then returned the accusation to their companions, and so it became a dispute. Therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do not dispute before Me﴾. The object of the dispute is omitted because "do not dispute" indicates it, out of preference for brevity in speech.

The prohibition of disputing after it has taken place is interpreted as a prohibition of continuing in it; that is, cease from disputing.

The meaning of the prohibition is that disputing about this is of no benefit, because the equality of the two groups in disbelief is sufficient for holding both of them to account equally, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The last of them will say to the first of them, "Our Lord, these are the ones who misled us, so give them a double punishment from the Fire." He will say, "For each is double, but you do not know"﴾ (Al-A'raf 7:38). This is a kinaya (allusive expression) meaning that God's judgment against them has been firmly settled, so their mutual disputing will not benefit them in shifting the burden of responsibility onto one of the two groups.

The basis for their equality in punishment is that the one who calls to misguidance is driven by what his soul desires, namely propagating falsehood without considering the evidences that restrain against it. And the one who receives falsehood from the one who called him to it is driven by what his soul desires, namely obedience to the leaders of error. So they are equal both in the caller and in the consequence of his call.

The waw in ﴿and indeed I had sent forward﴾ is the waw of ḥāl (circumstantial clause). The clause is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) referring back to the pronoun in "do not dispute", and it is a ḥāl that gives the reason for the prohibition of disputing.

The meaning is: do not hope that your pushing of responsibility onto others will save you from punishment, after I had warned you of the threat during your lifetime. Since you did not heed the threat, do not blame anyone but yourselves, for whoever warns has already given an excuse.

So His words ﴿and indeed I had sent forward to you the threat﴾ are a kinaya for the uselessness of disputing, since the punishment is just from God.

The bāʾ in "with the threat" is extra, for emphasis, as in His words ﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ (Al-Ma'idah 5:6).

The meaning is: I had sent forward to you the threat before this day.

[p. 316]

Taqdīm (sending forward) is placing something in front of something else. What is meant here is that it preceded the reckoning for associating partners with God, because God threatened them through the Messenger ﷺ.

So the first meaning, which was alluded to, is clarified by the clause ﴿The word is not changed with Me﴾, that is: I do not nullify that threat, which is a word (qawl), since the threat is a kind of speech. The definite article is for a known referent, meaning: what I threatened you with will certainly occur, because God has committed Himself not to forgive one who associates partners with Him and dies in that state.

The second meaning, which was alluded to, is clarified by the clause ﴿And I am not one who wrongs the servants﴾, that is: therefore I sent forward the threat to you.

The exaggeration in the description ẓallām (one who wrongs much) returns to the emphasis of the negation. What is meant is: I do not wrong anyone in any way; the meaning is not "I am not greatly unjust," as might be understood when a negation is directed at a restricted statement, which tends to direct the negation toward the restriction, because that is the more common usage. Most often, in the negation of intensive forms, the intended meaning is the intensification of the negation. Ṭarafah said:

"I am not one who lingers among the hills out of fear,
but whenever the people seek my help, I help."

He does not intend to deny that he frequently dwells among the hills; rather, he intends to deny frequency.

Al-Shaykh (ʿAbd al-Qāhir al-Jurjānī) in Dalā'il al-I'jāz mentioned that negation of a restricted thing is directed at the restriction itself, just as affirmation is, equally. However, the discussion of al-Taftazānī in al-Maqāṣid, in the section on the vision of God in the principles of religion, pointed to two usages in this. The more common is that the negation is directed at the restriction, so the thing negated is the restriction. But the restriction may also be considered a restriction of the negation, and this is the verified position.

Nevertheless, I hold that counting an intensive form such as this among restrictions is open to question, since what counts as a restriction is a word added beyond the negated word, such as an adjective, a circumstantial qualifier, or the like. Do you not see that it is not good to say "I am not a wrongdoer, but I do wrong," whereas it is good to say "I will not come to you as a warrior, but as a peaceful one"?

[p. 317]

Al-Zamakhsharī in al-Kashshāf has pointed out that choosing the description ẓallām here is a hint that, if the negated thing were not negated, it would be great injustice. For this reason it is said: there is no punishment except for an act for which there is a law preceding its commission.

( ﴿On the Day when He says to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Is there any more?"﴾ (

This is a temporal clause (ẓarf) dependent on ﴿He said, "Do not dispute in My presence"﴾ [Qaf 50:28]. The implied sense is: He said to them, in that saying, on the Day when He says another saying to Hell, "Are you filled?" The reason it is linked to that statement is that this saying to Hell is intended to terrify those being driven into Hell, so that they do not hope that, because of their great number, the capacity of Hell will be exhausted, and so that some of them will hope to be among those for whom no place is found in it. Allah has therefore related it in the Qur'an as a lesson for whoever among the polytheists hears it, and as instruction for the believers who recite the Qur'an. For this reason the reading of (yaqūlu) with the letter yā' is equally valid. It is the reading of Nāfi' and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim, following the apparent sense of what precedes it, namely His saying, ﴿He said, "Do not dispute in My presence"﴾ [Qaf 50:28]. The reading of the rest with nūn is an iltifāt (a shift in grammatical person, i.e., a turn from third person to first person), or rather it is an iltifāt that follows from the change in the mode of reporting, from speaking about an absent party to addressing a present one.

The first saying is literal: it is speech that proceeds from Allah by His sheer creative act, without any intermediary. For this reason it is attributed to Allah, just as one says "the Qur'an is the speech of Allah."

The interrogative in ﴿Are you filled?﴾ is used to alert the people of punishment to this question, by way of indirect allusion (taʿrīḍ).

As for the saying to Hell, it may be literal, in that Allah creates in the sounds of its flames sounds with letters from which speech is formed. It may also be figurative (majāz), an expression for the indication of its state by which it shows that it can contain what is cast into it of the people of punishment, in that its inner part is uncovered for those presented before it, so that they see its vastness, as in the words of the rajaz poet:
"The basin is full, and it says, 'Enough for me!'"
The interrogative in ﴿Is there any more?﴾ is used to express eagerness and longing.

In this there is an indication that created beings are eager to fulfil that for which they were created, as Satan said, ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray, I will surely sit in ambush for them on Your straight path﴾ [al-Hijr 15:39; al-Aʿrāf 7:16]. It also indicates the display of obedience to what Allah created it for, and that it does not hesitate or make excuses in carrying it out, in the most perfect condition of its kind.

al-Mazīd is a mīmī verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī), meaning increase, like al-Majīd and al-Ḥamīd. It may also be a passive participle (ism mafʿūl) from zāda, meaning: is there any further group of others who will be cast into me?

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 50, verses 31–35:

﴿And Paradise will be brought near to the God-fearing, not far off.﴾ ﴿This is what you were promised, for every constant returner (to God), keeper (of His commands).﴾ ﴿Whoever feared the Most Merciful unseen and came with a heart turning back (to Him).﴾ ﴿Enter it in peace; this is the day of eternity.﴾ ﴿For them there is whatever they will, therein, and with Us is more.﴾

"Wa uzlifat" is coordinated with "yaqulu li-jahannama" (the verse "On the Day We say to Hell, 'Are you filled?'"). The implied sense is: "on the day when Paradise is brought near to the God-fearing," and this is a return to the counterpart of the state of the misguided on the day the Trumpet is blown. Thus this sentence is connected in meaning to the sentence ﴿And every soul will come, with it a driver and a witness﴾ [Qaf: 21]. Were it considered coordinated with that, it would also be valid, but its coordination with the sentence ﴿On the day We say to Hell, "Are you filled?"﴾ [Qaf: 30] is sufficient without that, especially given the length of the discourse.

Al-izlaf (ازلاف) is bringing near (al-taqrib), derived from al-zalaf (الزَّلَف), with a vowel on the middle letter, which means nearness (al-qurba). Its verb is by analogy of the pattern "fa'ila" (like فَرِحَ), as the verbal noun indicates, though it is not transmitted in their speech. That is, Paradise is made near to the God-fearing, i.e., "draw near to it."

Paradise exists before the arrival of the God-fearing to it, so its being brought near may be by gathering them for the reckoning in close proximity to it, as an honour to them, sparing them the hardship of traveling to it; or it may be an expression of facilitating their arrival to it by means not known in the customs of the people of this world.

His saying "not far off" favours the first possibility, namely: "not far from them." Otherwise it would become a verbal emphasis of "uzlifat," as one says "hasty, not delayed," and His saying: ﴿Pharaoh led his people astray and did not guide﴾ [Ta-Ha: 79]. Establishing a new meaning (ta'sis) is more preferred than the possibility of emphasis (ta'kid).

"Ghayra ba'id" is in the accusative as an adverb of place, considered as a qualifier of an omitted place-noun. The estimate is: "a place not far," i.e., from the God-fearing. This adverbial phrase is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of Paradise.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 50, verses 36–37:**

﴿How many generations We destroyed before them, which were mightier than them in strength, and they roamed through the lands. Was there any escape?﴾ ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart, or gives ear while he is a witness.﴾

This is a transition from argument to warning (tahdid), and it is conjoined (ma'tuf) to what precedes it. This conjunction is a transition to admonition (maw'iza) with what befell the nations that denied, after the argument for the possibility of resurrection, through His saying ﴿We know what the earth diminishes of them﴾ [Qaf: 4], and what follows from it, His saying ﴿Were We wearied by the first creation?﴾ [Qaf: 15]. In this conjunction is the threat that was summarized in His saying ﴿Before them denied the people of Noah and the companions of the Rass﴾ [Qaf: 12] up to His saying "so My warning came due." So the threat that came due upon them is annihilation in this world, and this is the content of His saying ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them, which were mightier than them in strength﴾.

The report conveyed by His saying ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them﴾ is an allusive threat (ta'rid bi-al-tahdid) and a consolation (tasliya) to the Prophet ﷺ.

The two pronouns in "qablahum" (before them) and "minhum" (of them) refer to something known from the context but not mentioned in the speech, as was previously stated in His saying at the beginning of the surah: ﴿Rather, they wondered that a warner from among themselves had come to them﴾ [Qaf: 2]. It is explained by His following saying ﴿So the disbelievers said, "This is a strange thing"﴾ [Qaf: 2]. His saying ﴿The people of Noah denied before them﴾ [Qaf: 12] and His saying ﴿Rather, they are in doubt about a new creation﴾ [Qaf: 15] follow this same pattern, and its parallels in the Qur'an are many.

"Kam" (how many) is khabariyya (informative), and its specification (tamyiz) is put in the genitive by "min," according to the original rule.

"Al-batsh" means power over others.

"Al-tanqib" is derived from "al-naqb" with a sukun on the qaf, meaning a perforation, so it would mean: they pierced [through]. It is used metaphorically to mean: they subdued and subjugated, that is, they disposed of the earth by digging, planting, building, hewing mountains, and erecting dams and fortresses. It thus has the same meaning as His saying ﴿They tilled the earth and developed it﴾ [Rum: 9] in Surah al-Rum.

The definiteness of "al-bilad" (the lands) is generic, that is, [they roamed] in the earth, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿who transgressed in the lands﴾ [Fajr: 11].

The "fa" in "fa-naqqabu" (so they roamed) is for consequence (tafri') from ﴿mightier than them in strength﴾, that is, by their strength and might they roamed through the lands.

The clause is parenthetical (mu'taridha) between the clause ﴿How many We destroyed before them﴾ and what follows it.

It is like the clause ﴿Was there any escape?﴾, as a consequential parenthesis appeared in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That, so taste it; and indeed, for the disbelievers is the punishment of the Fire﴾ [Anfal: 14].

The clause ﴿Was there any escape?﴾ is a comprehensive substitute (badal ishtimal) for the clause "We destroyed," that is, a destruction from which there was no escape. It is also permissible for the clause to be a new independent statement.

The interrogation is then one of denial (inkari), meaning negation, and for this reason "min" entered upon the noun following the interrogative, as one says: "There is no escape." This is close to His saying in Surah Sad: ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them, and they called out, but it was no time for escape﴾ [Sad: 3].

"Al-mahis" is a mimi verbal noun from "hasa," meaning he deviated and escaped, that is, they found no escape from destruction. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them; do you perceive any of them, or hear from them a whisper?﴾ [Maryam: 98] in Surah Maryam.

His saying ﴿Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart﴾ up to its end may have the demonstrative "dhalika" refer to the destruction of the generations, which were mightier in strength, and it may refer to everything that preceded: argument, warning, and admonition regarding the Day of recompense.

"Al-dhikra" is the reminder of the intellect, that is, reflection upon the conditions of those whom destruction overtook, so that they may measure their own conditions by them, and know that what befell those will befall them. This is an intellectual analogy (qiyas 'aqli) which the discerning person grasps of his own accord without need of a reminder.

"Al-qalb" is the intellect and the perception of things as they are.

"Ilqa' al-sam'" (giving ear) is a metaphor for intense attentiveness to the Qur'an and the admonitions of the Messenger ﷺ, as if their ears were cast down toward it, so that nothing else occupies them that they would hear.

"Al-shahid" is the one who witnesses, and the intensive form in it indicates the strength of witnessing the one who reminds, that is, the fixing of the eye upon him out of eagerness to understand his meaning from what accompanies his speech of gesture or facial expression, for looking aids understanding.

This circumstantial clause has been brought to indicate the conjunction of its content with the content of its governing verb, such that the one addressed is one who gives ear while witnessing. This is the state of the believer, so in the speech there is an exaltation of the believers' station and an allusion to the polytheists, that they are far from benefiting from reminders and lessons.

Giving ear together with witnessing awakens the intellect to reminder and consideration, if the intellect has any heedlessness.

The position of "aw" (or) is for division (taqsim), because the one who is reminded either is reminded by what the intellectual proofs indicate, through understanding the arguments of the Qur'an and through taking lesson from the proofs of the traces upon their people, such as the dwellings of Thamud. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So those are their houses, empty because of what they wronged﴾ [Naml: 52]. So His saying "give ear" is a precious metaphor (isti'ara 'aziza), in which the directing of the hearing toward those reports, without occupation with anything else, is likened to the casting of a thing to one who takes it. Such a one belongs to the category of "one who has a heart." Or he is reminded by what is conveyed to him of reports about the nations, such as the narratives of the earlier generations. It has been said that what is meant by "one who gives ear while he is a witness" is specifically the People of the Book, who gave ear to this reminder and bore witness to its authenticity, because of their knowledge of it from the Torah and their other books. In that case "shahid" is from testimony (shahada), not from witnessing (mushahada).

Al-Fakhr [al-Razi] said: The indefinite "qalb" (a heart) is for magnification and perfection. The meaning is: for whoever has an intelligent, aware heart that draws out [lessons] by its intelligence; or for whoever gives ear to the warner and then takes heed. He said "give ear" and did not say "listened" (istama'a) because giving ear means one sends one's hearing and does not hold it back, even if one does not intend listening; that is, the reminder is attained by whoever has hearing.

This is an allusion, comparing the polytheists to one who has no heart and to one who does not give ear.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 50, verses 41–43:**

﴿And listen, on the day the caller calls from a near place,﴾ ﴿the day they hear the Blast in truth. That is the Day of Coming Out.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We give life and cause death, and to Us is the final return.﴾

Undoubtedly the sentence "istami' (listen)" is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the sentence "sabbiḥ bi-ḥamdi rabbika (glorify your Lord with His praise)", so the command to listen is linked by the fa' (then) with which the command to be patient over "what they say" was linked. It is therefore connected to the consolation of the Prophet ﷺ, and what is heard can only be of the kind that concerns him and the punishment of those who deny him.

Beginning the speech with "istami'" conveys an arousing of anticipation for what follows, under every possibility.

The command to listen in its literal sense is a command to be silent and attentive.

There are three approaches of the exegetes regarding the meaning of "istami'". The one favoured by the majority is to take listening in its ordinary sense. Since what is mentioned after the act of hearing cannot be something heard, because the Day is not something that is heard, it is necessary to posit an object for "istami'" that is indicated by the speech that follows. So it is estimated: "listen to the call of the caller," or "listen to their news," or "listen to the Blast on the day the caller calls."

You may also make the verb "istami'" be treated as intransitive, meaning "be a listener." On this interpretation, the meaning of the command to listen is an imaginative representation of the Blast of that Day in the form of something already occurring, such that the addressee is commanded to attend to it immediately, like the saying of Malik ibn al-Rayb:

"Desire called me from the people of my affection and my neighbours, at Dhu al-Tabasayn, so I turned back looking."

Ibn 'Atiyya took "istami'" in a figurative sense, i.e., "wait." He said: because Muhammad ﷺ was not commanded to listen on the day of the call, since everyone in it listens. The verse is rather in the sense of a warning to the disbelievers, so it was said to Muhammad ﷺ: "Be alert to this day and watch for it, for in it will become clear the truth of what you have said." End of quotation. I have not seen anyone precede him to this meaning, and similar appears in the tafsir of al-Fakhr and in the tafsir of al-Nasafi. Perhaps the two of them had seen it, since they are later than Ibn 'Atiyya, and although they are from the East, books are transmitted between regions.

Al-Zamakhshari has another approach, and he said: that is, "listen to what He informs you of concerning the state of the Day of Resurrection."

Page 330

In that there is a expression of awe and magnification of the importance of what is reported, just as it is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal, "O Mu'adh, listen to what I say to you," and then he spoke to him after that. I have not seen anyone precede him to this, and it is a fine and subtle interpretation.

The proper way to apply the three preceding interpretations is that "yawma yunadi al-munadi (the day the caller calls)" be a subject (mubtada'), and its fatha is a fatha of indeclinability, because it is a noun of time added to a clause. It is permissible in it to be inflected or built on the fatha. The fact that the verb of the clause is in the present tense does not conflict with this, because the verified view is that this occurs in eloquent speech, and this is the view of the Kufan grammarians and Ibn Malik, and there is no doubt that it is the more correct. Among its examples is the Exalted's saying: ﴿God said: This is a day when the truthful benefit from their truthfulness﴾ (al-Ma'ida: 119), in the reading of Nafi' with fatha on (yawma).

His saying "yawma yasma'ina al-sayha (the day they hear the Blast)" is an appositive in agreement with "yawma yunadi al-munadi," and his saying "dhalika yawmu al-khuruj (that is the Day of Coming Out)" is the predicate of the subject.

You may also make "yawma yunadi al-munadi" an adverbial complement (maf'ul fihi) of "istami'," and its construction after that is clear.

You may also make "yawma yunadi al-munadi" an adverbial phrase in the position of a fronted predicate, and make the subject his saying "dhalika yawmu al-khuruj," and the estimated structure of the composition would be: "And listen: that is the Day of Coming Out, the day the caller calls, etc.," and the demonstrative would be merely for alerting, or it refers back to "yawma yunadi al-munadi," since it precedes it in wording though it is a predicate concerning it in meaning. The demonstrative is satisfied with verbal precedence, indeed it is satisfied with mere occurrence to the mind. In the tafsir of al-Nasafi it is reported that Ya'qub, i.e., al-Hadrami, one of the readers of the ten mutawatir readings, paused at his saying "wa-ist-tami'".

The definiteness of "al-munadi" is the definiteness of the genus, i.e., "the day a caller calls," that is, from among the angels, and he is the angel who blows the second blast, so the bodies come into being and the spirits of people enter them for the gathering. The Exalted said: ﴿Then it is blown again, and behold, they stand looking on﴾.

The nunation of "makanin qarib (a near place)" is for the sense of type, since the purpose does not depend on specifying it. Describing it as "qarib (near)" indicates the swiftness of the arrival of those called, and this is what the clause "the day they hear the Blast in truth" explains, because it is known that a call from a near place is not hidden from those who hear it, unlike a call from a distant place.

"Bil-haqq (in truth)" means "with truth," and here it is the gathering. It is described as "in truth" to nullify the claim of the polytheists that it is fabrication.

"Al-khuruj (the coming out)" means leaving a house or a town, and "coming out" was applied to assembling at the place of gathering, because when a people leave their land, it is said "they came out." It is said: "they came out with all their multitude."

The demonstrative was brought for the sake of magnifying the thing pointed to, which is the day they hear the Blast in truth, so the full care is intended in distinguishing it, because of its specificity to this great news. The apparent expectation would be to say: "It is the Day of Coming Out."

"Yawmu al-khuruj (the Day of Coming Out)" is a name by predominance for the Day of Resurrection, i.e., the coming out from the earth.

The sentence "Indeed, We give life and cause death, and to Us is the final return" is a concluding remark (tadhyil), meaning: this giving of life after We had caused them to die is one of Our affairs, in that We give them life and give life to others, and We cause them to die and cause others to die.

The intended point is His saying "wa-numitu (and cause death)," while His saying "nuhyi (We give life)" is for completing the meaning of God's disposal of creation.

Likewise it is so in the *mushafs* that we have examined, both eastern and western, which are old.

The reason for the name is that this word does not occur in this form in any other surah of the Qur'an.

It is Meccan by consensus.

It is counted the sixty-sixth surah in the order of revelation according to Jabir ibn Zayd. It was revealed after Surat al-Ahqaf and before Surat al-Ghashiyah.

Aims of this surah:

It contains the establishment of the occurrence of the Resurrection and the recompense.

The refutation of the claims of those who deny it and the Messenger's mission of Muhammad (ﷺ), and their accusation that they speak without verification.

Their threat of a punishment that will test them.

The promise to the believers of the eternal bliss, and the mention of what made them deserve that rank of faith and excellence.

Then the proof of God's oneness, and the proof of the possibility of the Resurrection, and that it is certainly going to occur, by means of some created things which they see and sense, indicating the vastness of God's power and wisdom, over what is greater than re-creating man after his annihilation, and that man was created only for his recompense.

And the allusion to the warning of what befell the nations that denied God's messengers, and the clarification of the complete resemblance between them and those.

And the instruction to these deniers to return to God, to affirm the Prophet (ﷺ), to renounce polytheism; and the Messenger's (ﷺ) excuse from the consequence of their aversion, and the recording against them of their ingratitude for the blessing of creation and provision.

And their threat for that, with the like of what befell their predecessors.
